definition: Effusive means expressing feelings in an unrestrained, gushing, overflowing way.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word effusive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know effusive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: Her effusive welcome — hugs, happy tears, and three toasts before dinner — left the quiet exchange student blinking.
Warm is weaker than effusive: a warm greeting shows real friendliness within normal bounds, while an effusive one overflows them entirely.
Cloying is stronger than effusive — cloying gush is so excessive it sickens the listener, while effusive display can still feel genuine, if overwhelming.

Gushing means pouring out emotion in an open flood — thanks, praise, or delight spilling out faster than anyone asked for. Effusive names the same overflow as a whole manner: an effusive person's expression, gestures, and words all run past normal restraint, not just the torrent of talk.

Unrestrained means without any holding back, and it can describe almost anything — laughter, spending, criticism, applause. Effusive is unrestrained feeling in particular, expressed in a gushing, overflowing way. A debate can be unrestrained; only an outpouring of emotion is effusive.

She sent profuse thanks to every coworker who had covered her shifts that month.
Effusive means expressing feelings in an unrestrained, gushing, overflowing way.
When the intern's small bug fix went live, the founder did not simply say thanks.
He called an all-hands meeting, compared her to the company's original architects, sent a bouquet to her desk, and posted three paragraphs of praise on the internal board — with exclamation points.
The intern, who had expected a nod at most, hid behind her monitor.
Colleagues agreed the praise was heartfelt but almost comically effusive.
A meeting, a bouquet, and three gushing paragraphs for one small fix show feeling overflowing far past any restraint — that unrestrained outpouring is what effusive means.

The bookstore owner introduced the visiting novelist the way a fountain introduces water.
She was effusive for a full ten minutes — clasping the author's shoulders, dabbing her eyes, and telling the crowd three separate times that this was the finest debut she had ever shelved.
The novelist, a quiet person who had hoped to read two pages and sign a few copies, studied his shoes through most of it.
Attendees disagreed afterward about whether the display helped.
Some found the enthusiasm contagious; others thought it promised more than any first novel could deliver.
The author later thanked her, carefully, in one sentence.
